Attendees: Jared (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Luca (Redwood SRE) — Samir, Eve, Tom (Aurelia)
summary: Technical deep dive focused on reducing 99th percentile latency for edge inference in Aurelia's multi-tenant on-prem deployment. Main threads: making KV cache prefetch + sharding robust under bursty access, tuning positional encoding decay (rope attenuation) for longer context Llama/Mistral use-cases, and evaluating MoE routing costs vs. dense model alternatives. Action items and a pilot plan were agreed.
transcript:
[00:00] Jared Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — we'll get started, um, quick intros?
[00:12] Samir Patel: Samir here, ML platform lead at Aurelia. We run a mixture of Llama and Mistral variants for customer-facing chat, latency tail is our main pain.
[00:20] Eve Zhang: Eve, infra, interested in what networking changes we need for on-prem.
[00:25] Priya Menon: Priya from Redwood, I'll lead the perf knobs and demo configs.
[00:30] Tom Becker: Tom on the eng team, we can share traces after.
[00:34] Jared Kim: Great. Quick agenda: KV-shard prefetch, rope/positional decay tuning, MoE routing cost tradeoffs, microbatch and quant notes, then pilot steps.
[00:48] Samir: To start, our 99.9th jumps to ~1.2s on bursts and spike—average is fine. We suspect cold KV cache misses and some NIC congestion.
[00:58] Luca Rossi: We also see intermittent packet drops between racks when bursts hit.
[01:05] Priya: Okay, two-fold approach — first smooth the KV miss storm with prefetch + LRU adjustments, second reduce per-token compute via quantization + microbatching. We have a playbook for KV sharding patterns.
[01:20] Tom: When you say prefetch, do you mean prefix prefetch or token-level lookahead?
[01:26] Priya: Both. For chat flows where user context shows recurring prefixes, prefix prefetch combined with KV shard affinity reduces cache churn. For variable contexts, we do probabilistic lookahead — sample the top-k next-token distributions and prewarm likely KV segments. Not perfect but it reduces miss rates.
[01:45] Samir: That sounds heavy — does that increase token compute or memory?
[01:49] Priya: Minimal extra compute if you bound lookahead depth and use low-res logits (quantized). The key is to do it strategically for sessions with high reuse.
[01:56] Eve: From a network POV, prefetch will increase east-west traffic. We are worried about burst egress in our VPC.
[02:03] Jared: Right — this is where shard placement and NIC tuning matter. Luca, any thoughts on queuing?
[02:08] Luca: We can bump RX/TX ring sizes and enable DCTCP; also isolate inference network with VLANs and set QoS to prioritize KV prefetch during warm-up. But we should measure before fully enabling.
[02:20] Priya: Agreed — we recommend a staged rollout: enable prefetch in sampling mode (metrics-only), then ramp up. We'll provide BPF probes and eBPF dashboards for RX/TX counters.
[02:30] Tom: For the models themselves — rope scaling. We've seen positional decay issues with longer contexts. Mistral seems to lose coherency past ~4k tokens.
[02:40] Priya: Yes, rope attenuation / decay factor tuning is model-specific. Llama variants can tolerate slightly higher attenuation due to their positional embedding style, while Mistral/Qwen sometimes need dynamic decay schedules.
[02:51] Samir: How do we approach tuning without retraining?
[02:55] Priya: Change the rope scale at inference — apply a per-layer multiplicative factor to positional embeddings, and evaluate on held-out prompts. Also consider hybrid: lower rope scale at early layers, higher at deeper layers — it's often good for long-term memory.
[03:10] Jared: We ran an internal test where layerwise scaling gained ~3-5% perplexity improvement at 8k context for a Mistral-variant. Quant and kernel selection matter too.
[03:19] Tom: Are there standard knobs in Redwood runtime to change rope per model?
[03:23] Priya: Yes, the config is surfaced per model version — you can set rope_scale, rope_decay_schedule and can rollback immediately. We'll include safe defaults.
[03:30] Eve: For on-prem, would changing rope scale break performance SLAs?
[03:34] Priya: It can change compute slightly if it enables longer KV cache reuse, but unlikely to increase latency — often reduced overall token compute due to fewer re-reads.
[03:44] Samir: MoE question — we run an MoE model on certain heavy flows. Routing costs are killing us at tail. Any advice?
[03:52] Priya: Two patterns: soft routing with token affinity (route only high-entropy tokens to experts) and hybrid fallbacks. If you can cheaply detect low-entropy tokens, route them to dense fallback or cheaper experts. That reduces expensive cross-device all-to-all.
[04:07] Luca: The network cost of MoE is the all-to-all for experts — we measured a 2.3x increase in inter-host traffic.
[04:13] Priya: Exactly. Also consider packing multiple small requests into a larger microbatch to amortize routing overhead. But that interacts with latency SLOs.
[04:23] Tom: Microbatch sizes — we currently use 1-2 tokens per request, can we safely increase to 4 without hurting user perceived latency?
[04:29] Jared: Depends on workload — for interactive chat, you can do adaptive microbatching: immediate flush for interactive flag, else wait 20-30ms to fill a microbatch. We have an adaptive batching middleware in Redwood that targets latency SLOs.
[04:44] Samir: Does that approach change quantization benefits?
[04:47] Priya: Microbatching actually increases throughput and plays nicely with int8/4 kernels — the kernel's vectorization improves. But be careful with kv-cache memory alignment when switching kernels.
[04:58] Eve: Speaking of kernels, what's the guidance on kernel selection between Llama/Mistral/Qwen?
[05:03] Priya: For Llama-derivatives, optimized fused attention kernels often win at 2k-4k length. Mistral favors chunked attention kernels at long contexts. Qwen has better perf on mixed fp16/int8 paths with our latest kernel pack. We'll provide model-specific perf matrix.
[05:20] Tom: Any gotchas for HSM/KMS integration with on-prem Private?
[05:24] Jared: Make sure your HSM has low-latency key unwrap; token decryption in the critical path can add ms if misconfigured. We recommend caching unwrapped keys in a secure enclave per host and rotating in the background.
[05:37] Samir: Back to KV sharding — how aggressive should shard count be relative to GPU count?
[05:42] Priya: Shard count should be a multiple of active worker threads; too many shards increases metadata overhead, too few increases contention. For Aurelia's cluster we suggest shards = 2x GPUs for even balancing and to allow fast rebalancing during host loss.
[05:57] Luca: We'll need automated rebalance listeners to avoid hotspots.
[06:01] Priya: Redwood's runtime supports incremental shard rebalance with minimal pause. We'll show logs in the pilot.
[06:08] Tom: On quantization — we've tried static int8 and saw some hallucination uptick for Qwen. Any tips?
[06:16] Priya: For Qwen, per-channel symmetric quantization with a small 4-bit residual for attention weights helps. Also do a calibration pass with representative prompts. For hallucination, always run an eval set with generation metrics (BLEU/ROUGE isn't enough — use factuality checks).
[06:33] Samir: Let's talk metrics to monitor during pilot — what dashboards do you suggest?
[06:38] Priya: KV hit/miss, shard hotness, per-host tx/rx, microbatch fill time distribution, token latency p50/p90/p99, expert cross-host bytes (for MoE), rope scale variants performance, and correctness/regression signals.
[06:55] Eve: We need RBAC + audit trail for config changes in Private. Does Redwood record rope config changes?
[07:00] Jared: Yes, all model/version config changes are audited; SSO via SAML integrates with role mapping. We'll send the SOC2 appendix as well.
[07:08] Tom: Any rough numbers on cost tradeoffs if we switch certain flows from MoE to a dense 30B Qwen variant?
[07:15] Priya: Rough ballpark — MoE can be 1.5x-2.5x more expensive in network and tail latency for our tests, but if you consider token quality per cost, sometimes a dense quantized Qwen 30B comes out cheaper because it avoids routing overhead. We'll include a comparative spreadsheet.
[07:30] Samir: Can you run a quick sketch of a pilot plan?
[07:35] Priya: Pilot: 1) Redwood SE runs on-prem benchmark with your trace (48h) in a staging cluster using our KV shard default; 2) experiment rope_scale variants (layerwise) with baseline; 3) compare MoE routing heuristics vs. dense fallback; 4) provide perf/regression report. Estimated 2 weeks.
[07:53] Samir: Sounds good. Any blocker on our side?
[07:56] Jared: Need network access for the staging hosts and the trace files, and approval for the pilot agreements.
[08:02] Eve: We'll get infra tickets in motion.
[08:06] Jared: OK — recap: Redwood sends KV playbook + perf matrix + SOC docs; Aurelia provides traces; schedule pilot next week.
[08:15] Tom: One last Q — when you recommend probabilistic lookahead prefetch, does Redwood provide a library or do we implement?
[08:22] Priya: Redwood runtime has an opt-in prefetch module we can enable in sampling mode; we can also share a standalone library for early adopters.
[08:30] Samir: Great. Thanks all.
[08:33] Jared Kim: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with artifacts and calendar invite.
[08:38] [meeting ends]
recap: Agreed pilot: Redwood to run 48h staging benchmark on Aurelia traces; main focus on KV-shard prefetching, rope_scale layerwise experiments, and MoE routing heuristics. Deliverables: playbook, perf report, pricing. Next sync: schedule after pilot run finishes.
